betterCitation: Rumi, Mathnawi, Book III, lines 95 to 97, in The Essential Rumi, p. 281 (trans. Coleman Barks, 1995)
reason:
This is the line I expected to break, and it held. I went at it believing it was one of Coleman Barks's unsourced renderings, the sort that travels as Rumi with no Persian behind it, and the verifier's evidence looked like it was covering for that: it cited chapter 27 of a Barks anthology while giving a URL to Nicholson's MATHNAWI vols 3 and 4, which is the sort of mismatch that usually means the Persian source was asserted rather than checked. It was checked, and it is right.

WHAT I DID. I downloaded the PDF of The Essential Rumi and extracted it with pdftotext -layout rather than trusting any quotation site. Three things came out of the book itself. (1) The contents list for chapter 27, 'The Turn: Dance in Your Blood', ends with the entry 'Dance, when you're broken open ... 281', so the poem is untitled, is listed by first line, is the last piece in the chapter, and is on p. 281. (2) The body text on p. 281 prints it in five lines: 'Dance, when you're broken open. / Dance, if you've torn the bandage off. / Dance in the middle of the fighting. / Dance in your blood. / Dance, when you're perfectly free.' The three lines the proposal takes are lines 1 to 3, character for character, including both commas and the apostrophes. The lineation is Barks's own and the proposal preserves it with the slash convention; each line head keeps its capital D. Locator, page, chapter number and chapter title are all correct, and 'the untitled poem beginning Dance, when you're broken open' is an accurate description of what is on the page. (3) The References section, under CHAPTER 27. THE TURN, ends with the entry 'Dance, when you're broken open . . . ,' III, 95-97. That is Barks naming Mathnawi Book III, lines 95 to 97 as his source, so the verifier's claim about the References is exactly true.

THEN I CHECKED BARKS AGAINST NICHOLSON, which is the test that decides whether this is Rumi or Barks. Nicholson's Mathnawi, Book III: verse 95, 'Dance (only) where you break (mortify) yourself and (when you) tear away the cotton from the sore of lust.' Verse 96, '(Holy) men dance and wheel on the (spiritual) battle-field: they dance in their own blood.' Verse 97, 'When they are freed from the hand (dominion) of self, they clap a hand; when they escape from their own imperfection, they make a dance.' Barks's five lines map onto those three verses one for one and in order: broken open and the bandage torn off from 95, the middle of the fighting and dancing in your blood from 96, perfectly free from 97. This is a free rendering, not a translation, but it is a rendering OF SOMETHING, and the something is a real passage of the Mathnawi. The attribution to Rumi survives. Note also what the comparison rules out: the shipped lines come from the half of 95 about breaking and the bandage and from 96's battlefield, not from the 'sore of lust' clause, so nothing indelicate in Nicholson is riding under Barks's wording.

WHY I STILL FILED A BETTER CITATION. The source line as the verifier would ship it names no work of Rumi's at all. It reads as though The Essential Rumi were Rumi's book, when it is a 1995 anthology of Barks's versions and the work is the Mathnawi. The house pattern already in the carry does it the other way round and names the original first: 'Li Bai, The Hard Road, closing couplet, The Jade Mountain, p. 70 (trans. Witter Bynner, 1929)'. Barks himself supplies the locator in his own References, so naming it costs nothing and asserts nothing he does not assert. My version is 100 characters, leads with the name, carries no dash, keeps the page, and keeps the translator and year whose wording is being used. I dropped 'with John Moyne' deliberately: the title page credits 'Coleman Barks with John Moyne' for the book as a whole, but Moyne's collaboration is on the Divan quatrains, and this piece comes through Nicholson's Mathnawi, so Barks alone is the accurate credit for this line. The verifier's longer form is not wrong, only less precise; either will ship.

GATES. shipped.js: shipped [], near [], rumi at 0 of 3 for the year, cap 3, not banned. Nothing on the misattribution list touches it; the Rumi traps are not in that table at all, and the one I was worried about, a Barks line with no Persian behind it, is disproved above. No speaker to name: it is the poet's own imperative, not a character's. Scope: thirteenth-century Persian poetry in a 1995 published translation, both before 1999. It is Sufi devotional poetry and not scripture, so the Library rule does not claim it, and the track has already shipped Shantideva, Saadi and al-Ghazali on the same footing. Publishable: 'broken open', 'torn the bandage off' and 'the middle of the fighting' are figurative and describe no wound; the literal line, 'Dance in your blood', is line 4 and is not being shipped, which is the right cut. The chapter title does carry 'Dance in Your Blood' into the source line, which an editor may want to look at, but it is the book's own chapter title and it is not graphic. Tag Poetry is the form of the work. Theme fit is the best of the three I was given: dancing when you are broken open and in the middle of the fighting is Courage in Trial with no stretching at all.
